name: Dub
def: Jamaican studio art of remixing reggae into bass, space and echo — the mixing desk played as an instrument, vocals dropped for cavernous effect.

traits.v: Mixing desk as instrument: drop-out, echo, reverb, EQ.
Heavy bass and vast spring-reverb and tape-delay space.
Stripped, version-based; space over song.

why: The studio itself becomes the instrument — drops, echo and reverb sculpt bass and space from an existing track.

name: Afrobeat
def: Nigerian fusion of Yoruba rhythm, highlife and American funk and jazz — long, polyrhythmic, horn-driven grooves with political fire.

traits.v: Interlocking West-African polyrhythm over a funk pulse.
Extended, vamp-based, slow-building jams.
Big band — horns, percussion, organ, guitars.
Static modal vamps.

why: West-African polyrhythm is locked to funk and jazz horns over long, vamp-based, gradually building grooves.

name: Hindustani Classical
def: The North Indian classical tradition of raga and tala — modal melodic frameworks over a sustained drone, improvised across long, meditative arcs.

traits.v: A sustained tonic-and-fifth drone (tanpura).
Raga — modal, microtonal, improvised.
A long, unfolding alap-to-climax arc.

why: Its sustained drone and long modal improvisation directly shaped Western drone, minimalism and raga-rock psychedelia.

name: Highlife
def: West African dance music marrying Akan melody and rhythm with jazz-band horns and guitars — buoyant, urbane and guitar-and-horn-led.

traits.v: Lilting palm-wine and dance-band grooves.
Interlocking guitars and jazzy horns.
Coastal West-African urban nightlife.

why: Its guitar-and-horn dance-band template is the bedrock Fela Kuti fused with funk to invent Afrobeat.

name: Ska
def: Jamaica's first home-grown pop — a skipping off-beat guitar 'chop', walking bass and jubilant horns fusing American R&B with mento and calypso.

traits.v: An off-beat 'skank' guitar chop over walking bass.
Bright, punchy horn sections.
Up-tempo dance.

why: Its emphatic off-beat guitar chop is the rhythmic root that slows into rocksteady, reggae and ultimately dub.

name: Reggae
def: Jamaica's defining groove — a laid-back tempo, a heavy 'one drop' drum-and-bass emphasis and an off-beat skank, carrying Rastafari and roots consciousness.

traits.v: One-drop drums stressing beat three; off-beat skank.
Deep, melodic, foregrounded bass.
Roots and Rastafari culture.

why: Foregrounding deep bass and a one-drop groove with space in the mix sets up dub's remix-the-space approach.

name: Burundi Drumming
def: The ceremonial drum ensemble of Burundi — two dozen or more large ingoma drums played in a semicircle, with a lead drummer at the centre calling the changes over a rolling, relentless low-drum pulse. A 1967 field recording carried it into Western pop.

traits.v: Large hollowed-log ingoma drums; a centre drum leads while the ring holds a continuous beat.
A heavy, rolling, repetitive pulse with unison accents on the lead drummer's cue.
Royal court ritual; recorded by Michel Vuylsteke and Charles Duvelle in 1967 for Ocora's Musique du Burundi (1968).

why: Heard in the West through a single field recording, its massed rolling tom pattern became 'the Burundi beat' — a rhythm UK new wave and post-punk drummers used in place of the rock backbeat.

tracks.why: The 1967 recording itself — every later Burundi-beat record starts here.
Michel Bernholc overdubbed piano and guitar onto the field recording; it reached No. 31 in the UK in 1971.

name: 2 Tone
def: First-wave Jamaican ska played at punk tempo and volume by Coventry bands on their own label — deliberately racially mixed line-ups making the fusion itself an anti-racist statement.

traits.v: Ska's off-beat chop driven at punk tempos.
Horn sections and organ over overdriven guitar and bass.
Shouted, toasted, traded between singers.
Coventry, the 2 Tone label, Rude Boy style and Rock Against Racism.

why: It runs ska's off-beat chop through punk's tempo, distortion and DIY label economics — the literal hinge between the Jamaican and British punk lineages.

tracks.why: Built over Prince Buster's 'Al Capone' at punk urgency — 2 Tone's founding single, on 2 Tone's first release.

name: Canzone Italiana
def: Italy's post-war popular song — bel canto-derived melody, orchestral or piano-led arrangement and lyric-first writing, with the Sanremo Festival as its stage and engine from Modugno through the cantautori.

traits.v: Open, sustained bel canto phrasing; the big held note as emotional climax.
Rich diatonic progressions with an operatic lift into the final refrain.
Verse building to a soaring ritornello — the chorus as destination.
Sanremo (from 1951), RCA Italiana, and the 1960s–70s cantautore movement.

why: Opera's melodic sweep and a poetic lyric tradition met the 45 rpm single, producing a national ballad style whose oversized choruses Italo disco later set to drum machines.

tracks.why: The 1958 Sanremo winner that took canzone to the world — its soaring refrain is the template.
Composed and arranged by Ennio Morricone — the film-score and canzone lines in one record.

name: City Pop
def: Japan's boom-era studio pop — disco, funk, AOR and jazz fusion polished into glossy, urbane songs about neon nights and coastal drives.

traits.v: Lush jazz-fusion extended chords.
Tight disco-funk bass and drums.
Immaculate big-budget studio session polish.
Bubble-economy Tokyo leisure culture.

why: It fuses disco groove, funk bass and jazz harmony into an immaculately produced Japanese pop language.

tracks.why: The algorithm-era rediscovery that made city pop a global genre decades late.

name: Desert Blues (Tishoumaren)
def: Tuareg guitar music of the Sahara — hypnotic, pentatonic assouf grooves born in exile camps, electrified and carried worldwide by Tinariwen.

traits.v: Loping camel-gait shuffle over handclaps.
Modal, pentatonic guitar lines in call-and-response.
Clean-to-fuzzed electric guitar over droning vamps.
Tuareg exile, rebellion and desert festivals.

why: It parallels the blues from the other side of the Atlantic — droning pentatonic guitar as memory, exile and trance.

tracks.why: The loping assouf groove that carried Saharan guitar music to the world.

name: Amapiano
def: South Africa's dominant dance sound — deep-house chords and kwaito swing over airy log-drum basslines, jazzy pads and shuffling percussion.

traits.v: Shuffling, swung percussion over a bouncing log-drum bass.
Lush deep-house and jazz chords.
Township-born, globally streaming dance culture.

why: It grows deep house's warm chords into a distinctly South African groove built on the springy log-drum bassline.

tracks.why: Its log-drum bassline became the sound that carried amapiano worldwide.

name: Afrobeats
def: The pop juggernaut of West Africa — a glossy, melodic fusion of highlife, dancehall, hip-hop and R&B (distinct from Fela's Afrobeat) that now tops charts worldwide.

traits.v: Mid-tempo, syncopated log-drum and dancehall-inflected grooves.
Melodic, pidgin-inflected singing and rap.
Lagos-to-global pop industry.

why: It scales highlife and Afrobeat's rhythmic DNA into a melodic, global pop language blending dancehall, hip-hop and R&B.

tracks.why: The crossover hit that proved Afrobeats could dominate global pop radio.

name: Afro-Funk
def: West and Central African bands metabolising James Brown — funk's syncopation re-rooted in local rhythms, languages and horn traditions.

traits.v: Funk syncopation interlocked with African polyrhythm.
Horn-heavy dance bands with hand percussion.
Lagos, Accra and Douala club circuits of the early 70s.

why: American funk arrived by record and radio, and African dance bands answered in their own rhythmic languages.

tracks.why: The Afro-funk record that echoed from disco to hip-hop to pop.

name: Ethio-Jazz
def: Mulatu Astatke's fusion of Ethiopian pentatonic modes with jazz harmony and funk rhythm — minor-key horn lines drifting over a slow-burning groove.

traits.v: Qéñét pentatonic modes carrying an unmistakable melancholy.
Slow, smoky funk and Latin-tinged swing.
Swinging Addis — the imperial-era Ethiopian club scene.

why: Astatke, trained in London and New York, voiced Ethiopian scales through vibraphone, horns and a funk rhythm section.

tracks.why: The defining Ethio-jazz theme — pentatonic melancholy over funk.

name: Anatolian Rock
def: Turkish folk melodies and the electric saz run through fuzz and psychedelic rock — protest-era songcraft in odd Anatolian meters.

traits.v: Electrified bağlama (saz) alongside fuzz guitar and organ.
Anatolian folk modes and asymmetric aksak rhythms.
Istanbul’s politically charged early-70s scene.

why: A generation electrified Turkey's folk repertoire through the psychedelic toolkit, keeping its modes and meters intact.

tracks.why: Saz and fuzz in protest — later sampled across hip-hop.

name: Zamrock
def: Zambia's 70s rock explosion — fuzz-heavy psych and funk grooves cut in Lusaka during the copper boom, sung in English and Nyanja.

traits.v: Blown-out fuzz guitar over raw, danceable rhythm sections.
Post-independence Lusaka — state radio quotas fostering local bands.
Funk and local kalindula pulses under garage-rock drive.

why: Copper-boom Zambia heard Hendrix and James Brown and built its own amplifier culture around them.

tracks.why: Zamrock’s founding statement — garage fuzz with Lusaka swagger.

name: Afro-Rock
def: African rock bands fusing highlife and polyrhythm with heavy guitar — the pan-African, rock-facing sibling of Afro-funk.

traits.v: Rock drive layered over highlife and traditional percussion.
Twin guitars, congas and horns in equal measure.
Pan-African bands touring Europe — Osibisa’s “criss-cross rhythms”.

why: Where Afro-funk answered James Brown, Afro-rock answered Santana and the guitar bands — polyrhythm under the riff.

tracks.why: Highlife horns and rock guitar in joyful criss-cross rhythm.

name: Japanese Psych
def: Japan's psychedelic underground — from Group Sounds fallout to blistering heavy psych and endless feedback-drenched jams, often more extreme than its Western models.

traits.v: Feedback, fuzz and echo pushed past Western psych’s limits.
Side-long jams from meditative drone to total freakout.
Tokyo’s underground — communes, art happenings, tiny labels.

why: Imported psychedelia met Japan's avant-garde and noise traditions, and the volume knob became a philosophical position.

tracks.why: Heavy psych as spiritual exercise — Japan’s answer to Sabbath, weirder.

tempoNote: Highly variable — meditative drones to full-blast freakouts.

name: Latin Psych
def: Psychedelia across Latin America — from Peruvian garage fuzz to Brazil's Tropicália — folding local rhythms, protest and pop art into the psychedelic template.

traits.v: Cumbia, bossa and Andean pulses under fuzz guitar.
60s–70s youth countercultures under authoritarian pressure.
Garage-band fuzz and home-built effects with local color.

why: Psychedelia arrived as both sound and permission — each scene bent it around its own rhythms and politics.

tracks.why: Tropicália’s fuzz-pop joy — psychedelia with a Brazilian accent.

name: Bossa Nova
def: Samba cooled to a whisper — syncopated nylon-string guitar, hushed vocals and jazz harmony from late-50s Rio apartments.

traits.v: The violão’s clave-like plucked syncopation over a soft 2.
Extended jazz chords — 9ths, 13ths, chromatic slips.
Intimate, vibrato-less, barely above speech.

why: It fused samba’s rhythmic DNA with cool-jazz harmony at whisper volume — proof that quiet can be revolutionary.

tracks.why: Gilberto’s plucked guitar pattern here codified the entire genre.

tempoNote: Counted in 2 — feels far slower than the number.

name: Baile Funk
def: Rio’s favela party music — Miami bass mutated into the tamborzão drum pattern under chanted MC hooks, raw and relentless.

traits.v: The tamborzão — swung 130 BPM kick-and-conga pattern.
Chanted, percussive MC hooks and call-outs.
Favela sound-system bailes and phone-speaker virality.

why: One drum loop, endlessly recombined with local voices, became a self-sustaining parallel pop industry.

tracks.why: The tamborzão pattern under favela storytelling — baile funk’s global calling card.

name: Funk Mandelão
def: São Paulo's street-party funk — minimal, distorted beats with heavy kicks and overdriven bass, built for car sound systems at the fluxos.

traits.v: Hard, often four-on-the-floor kicks under repetitive loops.
Clipped, overdriven low end and metallic percussion.
Short, repeated MC phrases used as hooks.
Fluxos street parties and paredões, cars fitted with large sound systems.

why: It took baile funk out of Rio and stripped it to distortion and repetition, the sound that later spread online.

tracks.why: The 2016 track that popularised the mandelão sound.

name: Brazilian Phonk
def: Funk mandelão and automotivo rhythms and vocals fused with drift phonk's cowbell leads and nocturnal production — short, distorted and aggressive.

traits.v: Funk automotivo beats and kicks.
Noisy, distorted mixes with drift-style cowbell and synth leads.
Short tracks built around drops.
TikTok edits and streaming playlists; producers in Brazil and abroad.

why: It joined two online-era scenes, São Paulo funk and drift phonk, and carried Brazilian funk to a global audience.

tracks.why: The track that named the style and drew wide attention to it.
